STEP 3: Load and Prepare Dataset keyboard_arrow_down import numpy as np from PIL import Image import torch def get_bbox_from_mask(mask): objs = np.unique(mask) objs = objs[1:] boxes = [] for obj in objs: pos = np.where(mask == obj) xmin, xmax = np.min(pos), np.max(pos) ymin, ymax = np.min(pos), np.max(pos) boxes.append([xmin, ymin, xmax, ymax]) return boxes img = Image.open("PennFudanPed/PNGImages/FudanPed00001.png") mask = np.array(Image.open("PennFudanPed/PedMasks/FudanPed00001_mask.png")) boxes = get_bbox_from_mask(mask) --- [Page/Slide 3: img_tensor = torch.tensor(np.array(img)).permute(2,0,1)/255.0] --- img_tensor = torch.tensor(np.array(img)).permute(2,0,1)/255.0 Explanation: Converts mask → bounding boxes Converts image → tensor Prepares data for model The dataset gives: Images Masks (pixel-level annotations) But Fast R-CNN needs: Bounding boxes (rectangles around objects) So we convert: Mask → Bounding Boxes → Model Input Reads the image → actual picture (pedestrian scene) Reads the mask → shows where each person is (highlighted regions) Finds individual objects

→ each person has a unique value in the mask Creates bounding boxes → draws a rectangle around each person Converts image into tensor → model understands only numerical data Mask = pixel-level information Bounding box = object-level information TRANSFER LEARNING CONCEPT We use a pretrained model instead of training from scratch. Why? Already trained on large dataset (COCO) Knows general features (edges, shapes) We reuse this knowledge This is called Transfer Learning STEP 4: Load Fast R-CNN Model keyboard_arrow_down import torchvision from torchvision.models.detection import fasterrcnn_resnet50_fpn model = fasterrcnn_resnet50_fpn(pretrained=True) model.eval() --- [Page/Slide 4: )] --- ) ) (fpn): FeaturePyramidNetwork( (inner_blocks): ModuleList( (0): Conv2dNormActivation( (0): Conv2d(256, 256, kernel_size=(1, 1), stride=(1, 1)) ) (1): Conv2dNormActivation( (0): Conv2d(512, 256, kernel_size=(1, 1), stride=(1, 1)) ) (2): Conv2dNormActivation( (0): Conv2d(1024, 256, kernel_size=(1, 1), stride=(1, 1)) ) (3): Conv2dNormActivation( (0): Conv2d(2048, 256, kernel_size=(1, 1), stride=(1, 1))

) ) (layer_blocks): ModuleList( (0-3): 4 x Conv2dNormActivation( (0): Conv2d(256, 256, kernel_size=(3, 3), stride=(1, 1), padding=(1, 1)) ) ) (extra_blocks): LastLevelMaxPool() ) ) (rpn): RegionProposalNetwork( (anchor_generator): AnchorGenerator() (head): RPNHead( (conv): Sequential( (0): Conv2dNormActivation( (0): Conv2d(256, 256, kernel_size=(3, 3), stride=(1, 1), padding=(1, 1)) (1): ReLU(inplace=True) ) ) (cls_logits): Conv2d(256, 3, kernel_size=(1, 1), stride=(1, 1)) (bbox_pred): Conv2d(256, 12, kernel_size=(1, 1), stride=(1, 1)) ) ) (roi_heads): RoIHeads( (box_roi_pool): MultiScaleRoIAlign(featmap_names=['0', '1', '2', '3'], output_size=(7, 7), sampling_ratio=2) (box_head): TwoMLPHead( (fc6): Linear(in_features=12544, out_features=1024, bias=True) (fc7): Linear(in_features=1024, out_features=1024, bias=True) ) (box_predictor): FastRCNNPredictor( Explanation: Loads pretrained Fast R-CNN Uses ResNet50 backbone .eval() → inference mode STEP 5: Perform Inference keyboard_arrow_down

from torchvision.transforms import functional as F img_tensor = F.to_tensor(img) with torch.no_grad(): prediction = model([img_tensor]) Explanation: Converts image → tensor Passes image to model Gets predictions torch.no_grad() → faster inference STEP 6: Understand Output keyboard_arrow_down print(prediction) [{'boxes': tensor([[419.6865, 170.0683, 536.0842, 493.7453], [159.0727, 180.3605, 298.8194, 434.4604], [439.7836, 222.6208, 452.0138, 271.8359], --- [Page/Slide 5: [444.3562, 224.4628, 456.1511, 265.5336],] --- [444.3562, 224.4628, 456.1511, 265.5336], [437.7808, 226.5965, 446.2904, 271.2691]]), 'labels': tensor([ 1,  1, 32, 32, 32]), 'scores': tensor([0.9997, 0.9996 Explanation: Output contains: boxes → object locations labels → class IDs scores → confidence STEP 7: Visualization keyboard_arrow_down (np.float64(-0.5), np.float64(558.5), np.float64(535.5), np.float64(-0.5)) import cv2 import matplotlib.pyplot as plt img_np = np.array(img) for i, box in enumerate(prediction['boxes']): score = prediction['scores'][i] if score > 0.5: x1, y1, x2, y2 = map(int, box.tolist()) cv2.rectangle(img_np, (x1,y1), (x2,y2), (255,0,0), 2) plt.imshow(img_np) plt.title("Fast R-CNN Detection")

plt.axis('off') Explanation: Draws bounding boxes Filters low-confidence detections Displays final result STEP 8: Results Visualization (Confidence Scores) keyboard_arrow_down import cv2 import numpy as np import matplotlib.pyplot as plt img_np = np.array(img) for i, box in enumerate(prediction['boxes']): score = prediction['scores'][i] if score > 0.5: x1, y1, x2, y2 = map(int, box.tolist()) --- [Page/Slide 6: (np.float64(-0.5), np.float64(558.5), np.float64(535.5), np.float64(-0.5))] --- (np.float64(-0.5), np.float64(558.5), np.float64(535.5), np.float64(-0.5)) # Draw bounding box cv2.rectangle(img_np, (x1, y1), (x2, y2), (255, 0, 0), 2) # Put confidence score text label = f"{score:.2f}" cv2.putText( img_np, label, (x1, y1 - 10), cv2.FONT_HERSHEY_SIMPLEX, 0.5, (255, 0, 0), 2 ) plt.imshow(img_np) plt.title("Fast R-CNN Detection with Confidence Scores") plt.axis('off') Explanation: Shows confidence of detections Helps analyze model performance STEP 9: Measure Inference Time

Explanation Passes image to YOLO Model detects objects in one pass Stores results internally STEP 12: Visualize YOLO with Confidence Scores keyboard_arrow_down import cv2 import matplotlib.pyplot as plt img = cv2.imread("PennFudanPed/PNGImages/FudanPed00001.png") img = cv2.cvtColor(img, cv2.COLOR_BGR2RGB) --- [Page/Slide 8: (np.float64(-0.5), np.float64(558.5), np.float64(535.5), np.float64(-0.5))] --- (np.float64(-0.5), np.float64(558.5), np.float64(535.5), np.float64(-0.5)) for result in results: boxes = result.boxes.xyxy scores = result.boxes.conf for box, score in zip(boxes, scores): x1, y1, x2, y2 = map(int, box.tolist()) # Draw box cv2.rectangle(img, (x1,y1), (x2,y2), (0,255,0), 2) # Add confidence label = f"{score:.2f}" cv2.putText(img, label, (x1, y1-10), cv2.FONT_HERSHEY_SIMPLEX, 0.5, (0,255,0), 2) plt.imshow(img) plt.title("YOLO Detection with Confidence") plt.axis('off') Explanation Draws bounding boxes (green) Adds confidence score Similar visualization as Fast R-CNN STEP 13: Measure YOLO Inference Time keyboard_arrow_down import time start = time.time() yolo_model.predict("PennFudanPed/PNGImages/FudanPed00001.png", verbose=False) yolo_time = time.time() - start

print("YOLO Time:", yolo_time) YOLO Time: 0.22640252113342285 Explanation Measures how fast YOLO predicts Used for comparison STEP 15: Comparison Graph keyboard_arrow_down import matplotlib.pyplot as plt models = ["YOLO", "Fast R-CNN"] times = [yolo_time, frcnn_time] --- [Page/Slide 9: plt.bar(models, times)] --- plt.bar(models, times) plt.title("Inference Time Comparison") plt.ylabel("Time (seconds)") plt.show() Explanation Visual comparison of speed YOLO bar → smaller (faster) Fast R-CNN → larger (slower) **KEY OBSERVATION ** YOLO: Detects objects in one step Faster inference Fast R-CNN: Uses region proposals + classification More computation → slower YOLO → best for real-time applications Fast R-CNN → best for high-accuracy tasks “YOLO performs object detection in a single pass making it faster, while Fast R- CNN uses a multi-stage pipeline resulting in higher accuracy but slower inference.”
